external_ask: Search for full-text peer-reviewed publications from the DIET trial (NCT04645680) reporting: (1) human gut microbiome taxa or functional pathway changes associated with the high-fiber intervention, (2) statistical mediation analysis linking these microbiome changes to clinical efficacy outcomes (ORR, PFS, OS) in ICI-treated patients, or (3) explicit statements that microbiome mediation data is pending publication or unavailable. Also search for other human dietary intervention trials in ICI-treated solid tumor patients that report microbiome mediation of clinical outcomes.
limits: Statistical mediation analysis linking specific human microbiome taxa or functional pathway changes to ICI clinical outcomes (ORR, PFS, OS) within the DIET trial or similar human dietary intervention studies; explicit statement on whether such mediation data is pending or unavailable.
question: Does the DIET trial (NCT04645680) or other human dietary intervention trials report specific gut microbiome compositional or functional changes that statistically mediate the observed clinical efficacy improvements in ICI-treated patients?

usable_content: This study reports specific gut microbiome compositional and functional changes associated with a medically supervised ketogenic diet (MSKD) intervention in humans. Taxonomical findings include significant enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila (p=0.017931), Intestinimonas butyriciproducens (p=3.09E-05), Streptococcus thermophilus (p=1.15E-05), Roseburia hominis (p=3.94E-05), and Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus (p=7.28E-19) in the MSKD group compared to standard diet. Functional profiling identified increased phosphatidate metabolism (PWY-7039) and allantoin degradation (PWY-5705), with reduced L-ascorbate biosynthesis (PWY-6415). The authors note that Akkermansia muciniphila is linked to improved response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in existing literature. The study demonstrates that dietary intervention can produce sustained microbiome changes during cancer therapy, with MSKD patients showing better overall treatment responses and distinct microbiome profiles throughout therapy. This study explicitly states in the Discussion section that 'Subsequent mediation analysis on gut microbiome was not able to be performed' due to limitations including small sample size for dietary data (N=34). It reports observational associations between baseline dietary patterns (specifically high fat and dairy intake) and gut microbiome composition (e.g., Firmicutes unclassified, Ruminococcaceae, Intestinimonas, Enterobacteriaceae) with ICI clinical outcomes (PFS, HPD status) in NSCLC patients. The authors note that while dietary patterns were associated with HPD, the sample size prevented statistical significance for diet-outcome links and precluded mediation modeling. This study reports secondary objectives from the DIET trial (NCT04645680), a randomized controlled feeding study in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). The authors found that a high fiber diet reduced unconjugated secondary bile acids and secondary-to-primary bile acid ratios in serum compared to control. The authors attribute these metabolic changes to reduced gut microbiota-mediated biotransformation of primary bile acids (cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid) into secondary bile acids (deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid). In mouse avatar models using fecal microbiota transplant from trial participants, recipients of post-high fiber diet microbiota showed improved ICB response and decreased secondary-to-primary bile acid ratios. The authors conclude that dietary fiber modulates microbiome-mediated secondary bile acid synthesis linked to ICB response. This study reports secondary objectives of the DIET trial (NCT04645680), a phase II randomized double-blinded dietary intervention in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Patients were randomized (2:1) to a high fiber diet (30-50 g/d) or healthy control diet (20 g/d). The authors measured peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) using NanoString gene expression and CyTOF mass cytometry. Findings included decreased abundance scores of circulating macrophages, neutrophils, classical monocytes, and dendritic cells, alongside higher T cell activation gene signatures in the high fiber arm versus control within week 5-8. Human-to-mouse fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) studies using patient stool collected pre or post intervention revealed improved ICB response in mice receiving post-high fiber diet stool, suggesting microbiome-dependent benefits. This study is a protocol publication for the DIET trial (NCT04645680), a randomized, double-blind, controlled feeding study comparing a high-fiber dietary intervention (50 g/day) to a control diet (20 g/day) in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade. The authors explicitly state in the Data Availability section that 'No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study,' which serves as an explicit statement that microbiome mediation data is currently pending/unavailable in this report (addressing success criterion 3). The text details the planned methodology to address the gap, including whole-genome shotgun sequencing of stool samples, metabolomic profiling (SCFAs, bile acids), and planned statistical analyses to explore associations between microbiome profiles and clinical outcomes (ORR, PFS). This study is a protocol publication for the DIET trial (NCT04645680), a phase II randomized controlled feeding study in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). It details the study design comparing a high-fiber dietary intervention (50 g/day) versus a control diet (20 g/day). The authors explicitly state the primary objective is to establish effects on gut microbiome structure and function, and exploratory objectives include assessing associations with disease outcomes (ORR, PFS). The planned analysis involves longitudinal microbiome profiling (WGS sequencing) and statistical comparisons (linear mixed effects models, correlations) to explore associations between microbiome profiles and immunity/outcomes. Crucially, the Data Availability section states 'No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study,' indicating that results regarding microbiome mediation are not contained in this document. This study investigated a 6-week whole-food-based high-fiber dietary intervention in 10 melanoma survivors, utilizing whole genome sequencing and microbial association network analysis (NetCoMi). It reported specific microbiome compositional changes, including increased community connectivity and increased centrality of known fiber-responsive and Short Chain Fatty Acid (SCFA)-producing taxa. The authors identified Ruminococcus bromii and Dorea longicatena as potential keystone species consistently showing increased centrality and associations with fiber-responsive taxa across different association statistics. These findings provide specific candidate taxa and functional groups (SCFA producers) that could be relevant for mediation analyses in ICI-treated populations. This study reports an observational cohort analysis (n=128 for survival analysis, n=438 for profiling) in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). The authors found that higher dietary fiber intake was associated with significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS), while the use of over-the-counter probiotic supplements was associated with impaired response. The study included fecal microbiota profiling and parallel preclinical mouse models. In mice, low-fiber diet or probiotic use led to impaired anti-PD-1 treatment response and a lower frequency of interferon-γ–positive cytotoxic T cells in the tumor microenvironment. The authors state that gut bacteria modulate ICB response but the mechanisms underlying microbiota effects are presently unclear.
